artworks.title: Aurora Taking Leave of Tithonus
artworks.description: Solimena's Getty canvas: Eos rises from Tithonus' bed into her chariot — the dawn goddess leaving the Trojan prince she made immortal but not forever young.

artworks.title: Aurora and Tithonus
artworks.description: Ricci's Royal Collection oil: Aurora and the aging Tithonus — Venetian light on the myth of immortality without youth.

artworks.title: Aurora and Tithonus
artworks.description: Giovanni da San Giovanni's Florentine take: the dawn goddess and her Trojan lover — Baroque tenderness before the cicada fate.

artworks.title: Eos and Tithonos (kylix)
artworks.description: Boston MFA red-figure kylix: Eos pursues young Tithonus — the love story before immortality, painted for a symposium cup.

popCulture.title: Tithonus
popCulture.creator: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
popCulture.description: Tennyson's dramatic monologue — "The woods decay, the woods decay and fall" — remains the defining modern voice of the immortal who cannot die.

popCulture.title: Homeric Hymns
popCulture.description: Hymn 5 to Aphrodite: Eos asks Zeus for Tithonus' immortality and forgets to ask for youth — the canonical Greek telling of the dawn's tragic gift.

popCulture.title: Tithonus
popCulture.description: Trojan prince beloved by Eos — granted eternal life, denied eternal youth, and in some tellings turned into a cicada.
